title: Urge surfing
summary: Urges are waves. You don't have to fight them, just ride them out.
body:
An urge to gamble can feel like it will keep growing until you give in. It won't. Urges behave like waves: they build, peak, and then fade, usually within 15 to 30 minutes.

## How to surf an urge
- Notice it. Say to yourself: "I'm having an urge to gamble." Naming it creates a little distance.
- Find it in your body. Is it a tight chest, restless hands, a buzzing in your head? Describe it like a scientist.
- Breathe into it. Slow breaths, longer on the way out than the way in.
- Watch it change. Rate it from 0 to 10 every few minutes. You'll see it rise, then fall.

## Why it works
Every time you ride out an urge without acting on it, your brain learns that the urge is not an order. Over weeks, urges become weaker and less frequent. Every urge you surf is practice.

Use the SOS button whenever you need to surf one. It walks you through it.

title: The house always wins, by design
summary: Every casino game and betting market is built so you lose over time.
body:
Gambling businesses are not lucky. They are mathematically guaranteed to profit.

## The house edge
Every game has a built-in advantage for the operator. In roulette, the green zero means the payouts are slightly less than the true odds. Slot machines are programmed to pay back less than they take in. Sportsbooks build a margin into every line, so even a perfectly balanced book pays them.

## Why short wins don't matter
In the short run, anyone can win. That's what makes gambling feel beatable. But the edge works like gravity. The more you play, the closer your results get to the built-in loss. Big winners are advertised. The millions of quiet losers who pay for them are not.

## The takeaway
There is no system, pattern, or strategy that beats a negative-expectation game over time. Stopping is the only winning move.

title: "I'm due for a win"
summary: The gambler's fallacy and other thinking traps that keep you betting.
body:
Gambling hooks into some very human thinking errors. Spotting them in the moment takes away their power.

## Common traps
- **"I'm due."** Dice, cards and slot machines have no memory. After ten losses, the next spin has exactly the same odds.
- **"I almost won."** Near-misses are often designed in on purpose. A near-miss is a loss, but your brain reacts as if you were close.
- **"I have a system."** Patterns in random outcomes are illusions. Systems change how you lose, not whether you lose.
- **"I'll win it back."** Chasing losses is the fastest way to turn a bad day into a disaster.
- **"I'm skilled at this."** Knowledge of sports or poker doesn't overcome the margin. Bookmakers limit accounts that actually win.

## What to do
When you catch one of these thoughts, label it: "That's the gambler's fallacy talking." Then open your reasons.

title: Chasing losses
summary: Why trying to win back what you lost makes everything worse.
body:
Chasing is betting more, often bigger, to recover money already lost. It's one of the clearest signs gambling has become a problem.

## Why it's so tempting
Losses hurt more than equal wins feel good. Your brain is desperate to undo the pain, and one big win looks like the fastest fix.

## Why it fails
Bigger bets don't change the odds. They just make losses grow faster. Many people's worst nights started with "just win back what I lost."

## A different way to see it
The money you lost is gone. It's a painful but fixed cost. The only money you can still protect is the money you have now. Every day you don't chase, you keep it.

If you've slipped, log it, then focus on what you'll do differently next time. No shame, just honesty and a plan.

title: Know your triggers
summary: Situations, feelings and times that make urges more likely, and how to plan for them.
body:
Urges rarely come from nowhere. They're usually set off by triggers, and most people have a handful of common ones.

## Typical triggers
- **Feelings:** boredom, stress, loneliness, anger, even excitement
- **Money:** payday, a bonus, a bill you can't pay
- **Places and times:** late nights, weekends, being home alone
- **Media:** sports matches, betting ads, social media posts about wins
- **Substances:** alcohol lowers your guard

## Make a plan for each
For your top three triggers, decide in advance what you'll do instead. For example:
- Payday → move money into savings and bills the same morning
- Big match → watch with friends who don't bet, or skip it
- Bored at night → have a go-to activity ready, like a walk, a show, or a call

The Insights tab shows which triggers come up most for you. Use it to update your plan.

title: Put barriers between you and your money
summary: Practical steps that make gambling harder when an urge hits.
body:
Willpower is limited. Barriers aren't. The harder it is to gamble, the more time an urge has to pass.

## Barriers that help
- Ask your bank about gambling blocks on your cards. Many banks offer them.
- Remove saved cards from your phone, browsers and wallets.
- Use self-exclusion schemes offered by gambling operators and regulators in your country.
- Let someone you trust help manage money for a while, or set up a joint approval for big transfers.
- Keep only the cash you need for the day.
- Set up automatic transfers to savings on payday.
- Turn on the Chitah blocker for apps and sites.

## It's not weakness
Using barriers isn't admitting you can't control yourself. It's being smart about when you're vulnerable. People who recover use every tool they can.

title: First steps with gambling debt
summary: How to face money problems calmly and one step at a time.
body:
Debt can feel overwhelming, and that pressure can push you back toward gambling to "fix" it. There's a better way.

## Step by step
- **Stop the bleeding.** No new gambling and no new loans to gamble.
- **Write it all down.** List every debt: who, how much, interest, minimum payment. Facing the total is hard, but it's the start of a plan.
- **Cover essentials first:** housing, food, utilities.
- **Talk to creditors.** Many will agree to lower payments if you explain and propose a plan.
- **Get free advice.** Non-profit debt advice services exist in most countries. Avoid any service that charges big upfront fees.

## Remember
Debt can be paid down. A gambling win almost never solves it, and trying usually digs the hole deeper.

title: Telling someone you trust
summary: You don't have to do this alone, and saying it out loud helps.
body:
Secrecy keeps gambling going. Telling one trusted person can lift a huge weight and make relapse less likely.

## Choosing who
Pick someone who is calm, non-judgmental, and doesn't gamble. That might be a partner, friend, sibling, or counsellor.

## What you might say
"I need to tell you something difficult. I've been struggling with gambling, and I'm trying to stop. I'm not asking you to fix it. I just don't want to hide it anymore."

## What they can do
- Be someone you can call when an urge hits. Add them in Settings, then Contacts.
- Help with money barriers if you want that.
- Check in with you now and then.

They may feel shocked or hurt at first. Give them time. Honesty is the start of rebuilding trust.

title: Filling the gap
summary: Gambling took up time and excitement. Here's how to replace both.
body:
When you stop gambling, there's often an empty space, both in time and in excitement. Filling it on purpose is a big part of staying stopped.

## Ideas that give a similar buzz
- Physical challenges: running, climbing, team sports, gym goals
- Learning a skill with visible progress: an instrument, cooking, coding, a language
- Competitive games without money: chess, board games, video games with friends
- Projects: fixing things, building, gardening

## Ideas for calm
- Walks, especially outdoors
- Reading, podcasts, films
- Volunteering or helping someone

## Use your savings
Watch the money-kept number grow on the Today tab. Set a savings goal for something real you'd enjoy. That's a reward gambling never actually gave you.

title: After a slip
summary: A slip is information, not failure. Here's how to get back on track fast.
body:
Most people who stop gambling slip at least once. What matters is how quickly you get back on track.

## Right after
- Stop. Don't chase it to win back the loss.
- Log it honestly in the app. Hiding it feeds shame, and shame feeds gambling.
- Be kind to yourself. Talk to yourself like you'd talk to a friend.

## Learn from it
Ask yourself:
- What happened in the hours before?
- What was I feeling?
- Which barrier was missing?
- What will I do differently next time?

## Then move forward
Your previous gamble-free days still happened. You proved you can do it. Your new streak starts now.

title: Getting professional help
summary: Helplines, counselling and support groups. You deserve support.
body:
Apps help, but people help more. Many countries have free, confidential gambling helplines and counselling.

## Types of support
- **Helplines:** free and confidential, often available 24/7
- **Counselling:** cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is well studied for gambling problems
- **Support groups:** peer groups such as Gamblers Anonymous meet in many cities
- **Your doctor:** gambling problems often come with anxiety, depression or sleep issues, and a doctor can help

## Some helplines
Numbers change, so check them for your country:
- United States: 1-800-522-4700 (National Problem Gambling Helpline)
- United Kingdom: 0808 8020 133 (National Gambling Helpline)
- Australia: 1800 858 858 (Gambling Help)

Add your local helpline in Settings, then Contacts, so you can call it straight from the SOS screen.

If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number right away.
